title: Never pushing
hookLine: practice is an invitation, for you and for others: in Sa'di's story Abraham drives out a guest, and God rebukes him
tomorrow: why did a king read a lost scroll aloud to everyone?

lines: HE DRIVES THE OLD MAN OUT.
cards: Someone you love finds a new diet, or a podcast, and suddenly every dinner bends toward it. The Persian poet Sa'di tells a story about Abraham and a dinner.

Abraham, the story goes, would not eat until a guest came to share his bread. One day he found an old traveler on the road and brought him into the tent. At the table, the old man didn't say God's name before eating.
He worshipped differently. And Abraham, offended, drove him out.

teach.b: Then a word came from God, and in Sa'di's telling it's a rebuke. I have fed this man all his life, though he did not know me, and you could not bear him for one moment?
Sa'di tells it in the Bustan, his book of stories in verse, among the stories on kindness.
Benjamin Franklin later wrote his own version, as a parable against persecution, and in his telling Abraham goes out, finds the old man and brings him back.
Sa'di was a Muslim poet, and the Qur'an says it plainly, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no compulsion in religion." One reading: faith that's forced isn't faith.

teach.h: BREAD FIRST, NO TEST AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: And the tent shows what welcome looks like in this story: food first, warmth first, no test at the door. That's what an invitation feels like. It smells like bread.
It sounds like a tent flap tied open. It doesn't follow you down the road. The surprise in it: in Sa'di's story, God is the patient host, and Abraham is the one who has to learn.
If a practice has changed you, the urge to push it can be strong.
But practice is an invitation, for you and for others. Set out the bread, and let people come in their own time.

how: Sa'di's Bustan tells the story of Abraham and the old guest among its tales of kindness, and Qur'an 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion. On a personal path, a practice is shared by example and by invitation, and left open.

o: only practicing with people who already agree with you
holding your practice as an invitation, never as pressure
keeping your practice a total secret from everyone

p: didn't say God's name before eating
you couldn't bear him for one moment?

s: in Sa'di's story, God praises Abraham for driving out the guest
God rebukes him: you couldn't bear him for one moment?
the Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion
"There is no compulsion in religion." (2:256, Pickthall)
if a practice changed your life, the kind thing is to push it on friends
here practice is an invitation: offered, and left open.

games.q: you've started saying a grace before meals. tonight your roommate, who isn't religious, eats with you. what fits Abraham's tent, as Sa'di tells it?
o: say yours quietly, and serve the food without asking anything of him.
ask him to join the grace; it's your table, your rule.
skip grace tonight so he never learns you practice.
games.why: in Sa'di's story the welcome comes first, with no test at the door. your practice stays yours, and the bread is for everyone.

practice: If there's something to drink or eat nearby, a glass of water, tea, a piece of fruit, hold it and take in its smell. Then set it down within reach of an empty chair, the way Abraham laid his table.
Sit with the open place, and with one person you've pushed lately.

wordCard.voice: Never pushing: holding your practice as an invitation, for yourself and for others. In Sa'di's story, even God doesn't push.

orig.note: Arabic, Qur'an 2:256: there is no compulsion in religion.

carryVoice: Keep this close: an invitation, with the tent flap tied open and the bread out. Until tomorrow.
